---
title: "Introduction to Python for Data Science"
author: "Tomasz Rodak"
---

This course is an introduction to Python for students who already program in another language. Rather than teaching programming from scratch, it focuses on what is characteristic of Python: its data model, idioms and standard tools.

Materials for the laboratory classes. New labs are published here as the semester progresses — see the **Labs** section in the sidebar.

## Scope

* core types: numbers, booleans, strings, lists and dictionaries; slicing and comprehensions
* control flow, loops and iteration; console input and output
* working with files and text encodings
* functions, docstrings and `doctest`
* exceptions, `assert` and unit testing
* functional style: higher-order functions, `lambda`, `functools`
* object-oriented programming and special methods
* iterators and generators

## Assessment

In-class written assessment, last class.

## Literature

All of the following are freely available online.

* [The Python Tutorial](https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/index.html) — the official tutorial.
* [Dive Into Python 3](https://diveintopython3.net/index.html) — M. Pilgrim; written for Python 3.1, but still a distinctive and demanding read.
* [Think Python, 3rd ed.](https://allendowney.github.io/ThinkPython/) — A. Downey; a gentle, up-to-date introduction.
* [Composing Programs](https://www.composingprograms.com/) — J. DeNero; the classic SICP approach to programming, in Python.
* [Automate the Boring Stuff with Python](https://automatetheboringstuff.com/) — A. Sweigart; practical, task-oriented.
* [Fluent Python](https://www.fluentpython.com/) — L. Ramalho; free extra articles and a glossary accompanying the (paid) book, for later in the course.
* [Python 3 documentation](https://docs.python.org/3/index.html)
